content: The publication Elimination is released biannually by the Regional Office for the Western Pacific. It provides detailed information addressing the necessary components for verification. To assist countries and regions in preparing progress reports, a structured presentation format can be used to include essential data and analysis. 1. Background Information: The initial progress report should include the history of measles control in the country. This includes the years of introduction for the first and second doses of the measles-containing vaccine (MCV1 and MCV2), the current immunization schedule, and any historical changes. It should also detail the evolution of strategies for measles control and elimination, relevant surveillance systems, and the establishment of case-based measles surveillance. The amount of historical data will vary by country, but more comprehensive information is beneficial. This data is often available from previous national plans and should include specific details, such as border areas with endemic measles transmission and routine immunization coverage. 2. Analysis of Recent Measles Epidemiology: A thorough analysis of recent measles epidemiology is critical and can be presented using maps and graphs. WHO’s measles elimination country profiles serve as good examples. Countries are expected to provide data at the second administrative level, and some may even provide third-level data. This analysis should include age distribution, immunization system performance, and characteristics of confirmed measles cases. For outbreaks, maps should highlight locations and events linked to virus transmission, such as hospitals or schools. Efforts to reach hard-to-access populations should also be described. 3. High-Quality Information on Measles Outbreaks: Countries must provide detailed descriptions of recent measles outbreaks, including response actions, outcomes, lessons learned, and plans to address programmatic gaps. Tables summarizing outbreak characteristics and responses may be used with modifications. 4. Source of Infection for Measles Cases: The report should analyze the source and method of confirmation for measles cases. Epidemiological curves can be color-coded to differentiate endemic, unknown, imported, and import-related cases. 5. Characteristics of Clinically Measles-Compatible Cases: Each country should describe clinically measles-compatible cases, including their location, age, immunization status, clinical signs, and other possible diseases. Maps showing clustering, if present, should be included. 6. Quality of Epidemiological and Laboratory Surveillance Systems: Information on the quality of measles surveillance systems should be presented, including performance indicators and actions to address any gaps in surveillance or laboratory capacity. 7. Population Immunity: A detailed analysis demonstrating high levels of population immunity is essential. This includes national data on MCV1 and MCV2 coverage, supplemental immunization activities (SIAs), and serosurveys. Countries are encouraged to analyze immunity levels by birth cohort. 8. Sustainability of the National Immunization Program: The report should outline national action plans and financing strategies to sustain measles elimination. This includes routine immunization, SIAs, and surveillance activities. 9. Genotyping Evidence: Countries must provide genotyping data to verify the absence of endemic measles virus transmission. This includes historical and recent strains, as well as phylogenetic trees when available. 10. National Verification Committee (NVC) Plan: Each country should develop an NVC plan, including member rosters, orientation sessions, annual review meetings, and field visits. The plan should also include preparation of annual progress reports and implementation of recommendations from the Regional Verification Commission (RVC). 11. Validation, Comments, and Recommendations by the NVC: The NVC should provide a summary of outcomes from the report review, including validation, comments, conclusions, and recommendations. This may be presented as a cover letter signed by all NVC members. 12. Post-Verification Needs: After verification of measles elimination, countries must sustain elimination and prevent re-establishment of endemic transmission. This requires maintaining high vaccination coverage (≥95%) with two doses of MCV, conducting high-quality case-based surveillance, ensuring laboratory support, and maintaining outbreak preparedness and response plans. Annual assessments should be conducted with assistance from the NVC or SRVC, and progress reports should be submitted to the RVC. The RVC will review these reports, conduct field visits if necessary, and provide feedback and recommendations to governments.
